tagline.text: St. John the Baptist Cathedral, Kalibo's Santo Niño shrine and the center of the Ati-Atihan festival

location.label: Location
location.text: Poblacion, Kalibo, Aklan, on Archbishop Reyes Street near the Aklan River, behind Pastrana Park

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (including the January festival)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱50~300 (per person, downtown tricycle and snacks, no entrance fee)

children.text: Kalibo Cathedral is the seat of the Diocese of Kalibo in Aklan, dedicated to St. John the Baptist, and a diocesan shrine of the Santo Niño. It began as an Augustinian mission in 1581, became a cathedral in 1976, and is the spiritual center of the Ati-Atihan festival every January.

The official name of Kalibo Cathedral is the Cathedral Parish of Saint John the Baptist, and it is also known as the Diocesan Shrine of the Santo Niño de Kalibo. It stands in the center of Kalibo near the Aklan River and is the seat of the Diocese of Kalibo. The diocese belongs to the Archdiocese of Capiz, and Wikipedia lists Bishop Cyril Villareal as its head. Pastrana Park in front of the church and the Aklan museum Museo it Akean are right beside it, which makes the cathedral a natural starting point for a walking tour of downtown.

The history of the church goes back to the early Spanish colonial period. In 1581 the Augustinians founded the Kalibo mission, and in 1680 the mission was promoted to a parish with St. John the Baptist as patron. At that time the town was in Barrio Laguinbanua in Numancia, about 2 km from the present site. In 1804 the town moved to its present location, where a church was built and consecrated, and in 1826 the church and convent were completed. On May 24, 1885, a great fire burned the whole town and the convent, and the convent was rebuilt in 1886. In 1947, after World War II, Archbishop Gabriel M. Reyes, who became Archbishop of Manila, took part in reconstruction and remodeling.

In 1976 the Diocese of Kalibo was established and the parish church was elevated to a cathedral. On June 14, 1990, at 3:41 PM, an earthquake of intensity 7.1 (as listed by Wikipedia) struck Panay Island with its epicenter at Culasi, cracking the brick walls of the church. Bishop Gabriel V. Reyes restored and improved it. Wikipedia classifies the architecture as Baroque and Modern and credits the National Artist of the Philippines Leandro V. Locsin with the design (his works list gives St. John the Baptist Church, Kalibo, 1993, and a church-history site says he supervised its repair and reinforcement from 1993, so it is known as a renovation design rather than a new build). It describes a modern building that keeps lines from the post-war church that recall earlier church styles.

The focus inside the church is the image of the Santo Niño (the Holy Child). The Ati-Atihan festival, held every January, honors this image, and during the festival pilgrims arrive from all over the country and abroad. At other times it is fairly quiet, and it is a good place to stop between Mass times to look at the building and the image. Because it is a place of worship, cover your shoulders and knees, keep quiet and refrain from taking photos during Mass. The name Kalibo itself is tied to the religious history of the area. According to the Aklan museum, in 1569 Legazpi and his grandson Juan de Salcedo helped the Ati people stand up to raiders from Mindoro, and many Ati were baptized in what is called the "baptism of the thousand." The most widely accepted explanation is that the name Kalibo comes from the Aklanon "sanka libo," meaning "one thousand." Walking through Pastrana Park in front of the church with this story in mind makes the plaza look different. The plaza also holds a historical marker for Aklan-born Archbishop Gabriel M. Reyes, the first Filipino Archbishop of Manila, and a monument to World War II veterans.

blocks.title: The Santo Niño de Kalibo image

children.text: The center of the church is the Santo Niño image, and the January Ati-Atihan festival is held in its honor. Its formal name as a shrine is the Diocesan Shrine of the Santo Niño de Kalibo.

blocks.title: The stage of the Ati-Atihan festival

children.text: During the Ati-Atihan festival, which peaks around the third Sunday of January each year, the church and the plaza in front fill with Mass, parades, drums and dancing. Festival dates change each year, so check the latest announcements.

According to Wikipedia, the designer is National Artist Leandro Locsin, and the work is reported to be tied to the renovation and repair that began in 1993. The building blends Baroque elements with a modern style, and its orange pilasters stand out.

The Augustinians founded the mission in 1581, it became a parish in 1680, and in 1804 the church was consecrated at its present site. The building has been rebuilt several times after fires, war and earthquakes.

blocks.title: Museo it Akean, the Aklan museum

children.text: Right next to the church is the Aklan provincial museum, which displays local history and culture and Ati-Atihan costumes. Check the museum's own information for its hours and admission.

The plaza in front of and behind the church has statues of Rizal and Bonifacio and monuments to local figures. It is the stage for the Ati-Atihan festival and is a pleasant place to stroll around sunset.

The church stands in central Kalibo near the Aklan River, so the market, restaurants and tricycle stands are within walking distance. It makes a good starting point for a half-day walking route downtown.
The Aklan Freedom Shrine, Museo it Akean and the market are all within walking distance or a short tricycle ride. Walking on from the church makes for a full outing.
Take a tricycle from your downtown hotel or the airport to the front of Kalibo Cathedral. Times when no Mass is going on are best for looking around.
Look around inside the cathedral quietly and rest for a moment before the Santo Niño image. Avoid taking photos during Mass.
See the statues and monuments in Pastrana Park behind the church.
Visit Museo it Akean next door (open on weekdays, confirm the hours).
Have lunch at a restaurant near the market and walk to the Aklan Freedom Shrine.
Mass times and museum hours can change, so check before you go.
If there is an early Mass or event, arrive early at the front of the church and find a place.
Watch the street parade and drums and take photos, but leave valuables at your hotel.
Rest and have lunch at midday, when the crowd is biggest.
Watch the evening procession and performances at Pastrana Park around sunset.
During the festival, lodging sells out months ahead and roads are jammed, so book early.
There are direct flights from Manila's Ninoy Aquino International Airport to Kalibo International Airport (KLO) taking about
1 hour
. Which airlines fly the route changes, so check the latest information when you book.
From the airport you can reach the town center by tricycle or taxi, and one guide says the airport is close enough that it takes about
10~15 minutes
One guide says it takes about
1 hour 30 minutes
from the Caticlan jetty to Kalibo by bus or van. Before boarding, confirm with the driver that you can get off in downtown Kalibo (Poblacion).
Tricycles are the main way to get around town. The cathedral, Pastrana Park, the museum and the market are all within walking distance of each other.
When you hail a tricycle in front of the church, say where you are going and agree on the fare first.
One guide says it takes about
4~5 hours
to Kalibo by bus from Iloilo City and about
1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours
from Roxas City. Check fares locally.
You can visit the church all year, but the dry season from November to May is best for walking. The midday sun is strong, so morning or late afternoon is easier.

The Ati-Atihan festival peaks around the third Sunday of January each year and is when Kalibo is at its busiest. Lodging and flights sell out early, so book at least two to three months ahead. During Holy Week, the week before Easter, there are also church processions, which show a quieter side of local faith.

Hotels cluster in downtown Kalibo around the cathedral and Pastrana Park (Poblacion) and along the road to the airport. During the festival you need to stay downtown so you do not miss the parades. If you have an early flight or arrive late, a hotel near the airport is easier. Room rates vary a lot by season, so check the latest reviews on a booking site.

Aklan food makes liberal use of coconut. You can try binakol, chicken simmered in coconut water, and inubaran, banana stem pith cooked in coconut milk. A market is said to be held on Sundays near the market, where you can buy grilled skewers and rice cakes (kakanin). The names and hours of restaurants near the church could not be confirmed, so look around on the spot.
Dress modestly, covering shoulders and knees, and avoid photos and loud voices during Mass.
Museo it Akean is said to open only on weekdays, so if you pass through on a weekend, plan around the church and the park.
During the Ati-Atihan festival many people will smear soot or paint on your face, so bring clothes you do not mind losing and a waterproof bag.
Most places around the church are within walking distance, so wear comfortable shoes, and bring a hat and water at midday.
Mass times differ by day and season, so check the church bulletin board or the parish contact.
Agree on the tricycle fare first and carry plenty of small bills in cash.
The museum, the Freedom Shrine and Pastrana Park can be combined into a half-day route with little travel.
The museum, church and park are minutes apart on foot, so rather than hailing a ride, walk and read the signs and monument plaques. Reading them takes longer than you might expect.
Putting a small amount in the church donation box is voluntary, and nobody will press you.
During the festival pickpocketing and lost items increase. Leave valuables at your hotel and agree on a meeting place with your group before you go into the middle of a parade.
The church is a place of worship, so avoid short shorts or sleeveless tops and keep quiet during Mass.
Mass times and opening hours can change, so check before you visit.
Opening days and hours for Museo it Akean differ by source (one says weekdays 8 AM to 4 PM and another says Tuesday to Sunday).
Lodging and airfares jump during the festival and at year-end, so book two to three months ahead.
Typhoons and the rainy season can cancel flights and flood roads, so check weather advisories.
The Aklan capital
Kalibo
, where the church stands, has a market, pineapple-fiber weaving workshops and a mangrove eco-park among other sights.
The
Ati-Atihan Festival
, which peaks in front of the church every January, is the signature celebration in honor of the Santo Niño.
Reached from Kalibo Airport via Caticlan,
Boracay
is the Philippines' best-known beach resort.
A mangrove forest park with a bamboo walkway, about
10~15 minutes
by tricycle from downtown.
